sections.heading: Why we are writing to you

sentences.text: We are writing because STX1B-related generalized epilepsy with febrile seizures plus and SLC6A1-related epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures appear to share the same broad disease road: too little protein from loss of function of one copy.
The measured phenotype similarity between the two conditions is high at 0.3082.
Because of that, some parts of registry planning, outcome planning, and network building may be useful to compare across the two communities.
Both gene-condition links have been confirmed in Gene2Phenotype, with strong confidence for STX1B and definitive confidence for SLC6A1.
For both conditions, the curated mechanism is loss of function, but this was inferred from variant types.

The shared informative clinical features listed in the pack are atonic seizure, generalized non-motor (absence) seizure, non-motor seizure, dialeptic seizure, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.
Both conditions also have published disease models reported in PubMed.

sections.heading: What we would like to learn from or reuse

sentences.text: The pack says registry design and natural history protocol are transferable.
The SLC6A1 studies listed for this are NCT07531511 and NCT01238250.
The pack also says outcome measures and endpoints are transferable, but age of onset and severity still need review before any instrument is adopted.
Clinical network, sites, and investigators are also marked transferable.
We would value learning how your community set up its organization, natural history work, registry options, and study relationships.

For STX1B, the pack did not find a patient organization, a registry or natural history study, active NIH-funded research in FY2025-2026, a targeted clinical trial, or an approved disease-specific therapy.

For SLC6A1, the pack found a patient organization listing called SLC6A1 Connect, two registry or natural history studies, two active NIH-funded projects in FY2025-2026, and three targeted clinical trials.
Neither condition has an approved disease-specific therapy in the pack.
We must not assume that a therapy approach, model, assay, or trial design will carry over directly from SLC6A1 to STX1B.
The reason is that mechanism is recorded per gene and disease, not per family, and a child's own STX1B variant may act differently.
That variant class should be confirmed with a clinical geneticist before acting on any transfer idea.
We also must not assume the apparent overlap is highly specific, because 100% of the shared phenotype weight comes from common, low-information terms.
We also cannot assume the SLC6A1 organization listing has been fully verified, because the pack says it passed only an automated check and no human has verified it.
The pack does not assert enrolment eligibility for STX1B families in SLC6A1 trials.
Does the overlap between STX1B and SLC6A1 go beyond common features such as seizures and developmental delay, in your clinical experience.
Is SLC6A1 Connect the right contact, and does it run a registry.
Has a child's specific STX1B variant been functionally classified as loss of function, gain of function, or dominant negative, and does it match the mechanism recorded for the condition.
What functional evidence exists for STX1B, given that the curated mechanism is inferred from variant types rather than functional studies.

glossary.meaning: A change that reduces how much a gene works or how much working protein is made.
A score that compares the clinical features seen in two conditions.
A study that follows people over time to learn how a condition changes.
A result a study measures to judge change over time.
A change in a gene's DNA sequence.
A doctor who helps interpret genetic test results and what they may mean for a person.
